body.heading: A reaction that feeds itself
paragraphs: Burning — combustion — is a fast reaction between a fuel and oxygen that releases energy as heat and light. Wood, petrol and candle wax are all fuels: substances whose atoms, rearranged with oxygen into carbon dioxide and water, end up holding less energy than they started with. The difference escapes as the fire.

Fire is self-sustaining once lit, because the heat it releases is exactly what neighbouring fuel needs to reach its ignition temperature and react in turn. A flame is this chain reaction made visible: a thin zone where fuel vapour and oxygen are reacting as fast as they can meet.

body.heading: Three sides of the triangle
paragraphs: Firefighters summarise the recipe as a triangle: fuel, oxygen and heat. All three must be present together, and removing any single side collapses the whole thing. This is not just a diagram — it is the operating manual behind every firefighting method ever used.

Water attacks the heat side, soaking it up as it turns to steam. A fire blanket or a carbon dioxide extinguisher attacks the oxygen side, smothering the flames with gas the fire cannot use. Forest firefighters attack the fuel side, cutting firebreaks — cleared strips the flames cannot cross — and letting the fire burn itself out against them.

body.heading: The right tool for each fire
paragraphs: The triangle also explains the warnings on extinguishers. Water on a chip-pan fire is a disaster: it sinks into burning oil, flashes to steam and throws flaming fat into the air. Electrical fires need non-conducting extinguishers, because water can carry the current to the person holding the hose.

A candle under a glass jar shows the oxygen side neatly. Sealed in, the flame consumes the jar's oxygen, weakens as the level falls, and dies when roughly a sixth of the air's oxygen is gone — long before the fuel, the wax, runs out.

description: Fire is a fast chemical reaction between a fuel and oxygen — and it only keeps going while fuel, oxygen and heat all remain present.
